extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency counsel, and policy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the legal standards and principles courts use to evaluate agency invocations of the APA's 'good cause' exception to notice-and-comment rulemaking and who should police compliance. Focuses on categorical justifications, multifactor tests, and standards of judicial deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory formulation of good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA permits dispensing with notice-and-comment when 'notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest' (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(3)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This textual formulation is the baseline for judicial review; courts apply the statute's open-ended language to fact-bound situations, producing variance in application. Scholars and litigants frame many analytic approaches around these three statutory terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite categorization of good cause uses
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonly used classification divides good cause cases into: (1) emergencies; (2) circumstances where prior notice could be detrimental to the statutory scheme; and (3) instances where Congress implicitly waived § 553’s requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy helps organize cases but can conflate factors; courts sometimes insert new considerations when applying these categories. Examples: emergency (FAA post-9/11 suspension of pilots' certificates); detrimental notice (price regulation in oil crisis); implicit waiver (statutory deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multifactor considerations for assessing good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly and judicial analyses identify multiple factual factors to weigh: whether the agency acted pursuant to a statutory deadline; potential harm from advance notice; economic harm from delaying notice-and-comment; harm to public safety from delay; whether the agency accepted/responded to post-promulgation comment; whether the agency issues the rule routinely; scope limitations of the rule; significant reliance interests; issuance pursuant to an injunction; whether the agency revised the rule in response to a court order; and whether the agency provided contemporaneous justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often apply a contextual, multifactor inquiry rather than a single bright-line rule. The presence or absence of these factors (and their strength) informs whether good cause exists in a given case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency/public-safety justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may invoke good cause in emergencies requiring swift action to protect public safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency is paradigmatic for good cause (e.g., D.C. Circuit upholding FAA post-9/11 rule). But courts disagree about the threshold level of threat required; agencies must present factual findings showing the urgency. Courts will not excuse emergencies of the agency's own making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-notice-subversion of statutory schemes (market/manipulation rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause can be justified when advance notice itself would precipitate activity by regulated parties that would harm the public welfare or undermine the statutory scheme (e.g., market manipulation by sophisticated actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have upheld good cause where announcement would cause price discrimination or other market dislocations (Mobil Oil/1970s price-regulation examples). The agency must explain how notice would lead to the specific harm alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit congressional waiver / deadlines rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts sometimes infer that Congress implicitly waived notice-and-comment when statutes impose tight deadlines or complexity that make advance notice impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines may justify good cause when they are 'very tight' and the statute is 'particularly complicated' (Petry example). Courts apply a contextual/multifactor analysis to deadline claims and generally reject claims where the agency created its own emergency by delaying action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/ad hoc whole-circumstances analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts analyze 'the entire set of circumstances' surrounding an agency action to decide whether good cause was properly invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because § 553 applies across diverse factual settings, courts typically weigh all facts and circumstances rather than apply a bright-line rule; this produces an inherently ad hoc quality to decisions and challenges administrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-and-capricious standard of review (deferential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many circuits review agency good-cause assertions under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard of 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), giving limited discretion to reverse an agency decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this deferential review, courts evaluate whether the agency offered a rational connection between facts and its invocation of good cause. Examples: Eleventh Circuit (Dean) upheld agency reliance on public safety and legal certainty under this standard. Several courts apply this standard without expressly endorsing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo review of legal conclusion of good cause (non-deferential)
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Circuit (Sorenson) announced that an agency’s legal conclusion that good cause exists should be reviewed de novo, reasoning that deference would conflict with congressional intent to 'narrowly' construe the exception and that agencies lack interpretive authority over the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sorenson applied rigorous scrutiny, requiring factual findings to support asserted threats; it nonetheless preserved deference to agency factual findings unless arbitrary and capricious. The Second Circuit has since cited Sorenson and applied 'exacting' review in at least one case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuits sometimes decline to specify a standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Some appellate courts extensively discuss the proper standard of review but ultimately decline to decide it, applying (without endorsing) deferential review or finding the agency's action deficient under any standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts like the Third, Ninth, Eighth, and D.C. circuits have at times avoided selecting a single standard, resolving cases on the ground that the agency's justification fails even under the most deferential review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that agencies provide factual findings/supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts expect agencies to substantiate claims supporting good cause with contemporaneous factual findings; unsupported assertions (e.g., speculative fiscal peril or 'surge' claims) are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sorenson rejected an FCC claim of impending fiscal peril for lack of factual findings; E. Bay Sanctuary Covenant found speculative border 'surge' claims too speculative. Agencies should document the nature and immediacy of harms to justify bypassing notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on agency-created emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause cannot arise from an emergency created by the agency's own delay or conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly held that agencies may not manufacture urgency by waiting until the end of a deadline or otherwise creating the conditions they later invoke as 'good cause.' Examples: cases rejecting agency-created emergency justifications (Nat. Res. Def. Council; Valverde; Ninth Circuit decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow construction / reluctance to countenance the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial interpretive principle that the good cause exception should be construed narrowly and with reluctance to excuse notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (and scholars cited by courts) emphasize that the APA favors public participation and that deference to agency invocations of good cause conflicts with congressional intent. This principle undergirds calls for closer scrutiny or de novo review of legal conclusions.
